concepts.statement_en: Under RA 7883, a BHW "voluntarily renders primary health care services" in the community after receiving proper training and accreditation from the local health board — the legal basis for the role, and the source of the Primary Health Care Approach as the guiding strategy and the barangay health station as a service hub.
concepts.source: INC-21's original Module 1 draft (displaced, git commit d424bde); reference-manual PDF 13

concepts.statement_en: Under RA 7883, a BHW may be given hazard allowances, subsistence allowance (isolated barangay health stations only), training/education and career enrichment programs, civil service eligibility, free legal services, and priority access to loans.
concepts.source: deck slide 19; reference-manual PDF 13; RA 7883 IRR via DOH BLHD FAQ (sources.json ra-7883-irr)

concepts.statement_en: To be eligible for RA 7883's benefits, a BHW must be registered with the local health board of the city or municipality where they render service.
The total number of BHWs nationwide must not exceed one percent (1%) of the total population (RA 7883 §5).

BHW Eligibility (BHWE) in the Civil Service is granted to BHWs who are accredited by the local health board, have completed a minimum of two years of college leading to a degree, have actively and voluntarily served continuously and full time for five years or more as an accredited BHW, and have a satisfactory service record. The five years count only after accreditation, only if unpaid except for an honorarium, and not before 20 February 1995; job-order and contract-of-service BHWs can still qualify (CSC Resolution No. 99-2845).
concepts.source: deck slide 20; reference-manual PDF 13; CSC Resolution No. 99-2845 (sources.json csc-res-99-2845)

concepts.statement_en: Under Section 5 of the RA 7883 IRR, responsibility for BHW registration and accreditation lies with the local health board.

The local health board's specific responsibilities include: safeguarding the registration and accreditation process; evaluating applications; recording board decisions in a resolution or meeting minutes; issuing certificates of registration/accreditation; reviewing and approving incentives that require local funds; recommending benefits and fund appropriation; providing an official copy of the local BHW registry to the DOH; and monitoring the services registered/accredited BHWs provide.
A local health board may create a BHW Registration and Accreditation Committee to evaluate applications, interview applicants, recommend action to the board, and prepare and update the BHW registry.

Module 4 maps to the TESDA BHS NC II competency 'Develop life and career decisions', whose outcomes are: manage one's emotions, develop reflective practices, and boost self-confidence and develop self-regulation.
